claims.text: Rapid quenching of a magnetic high-entropy alloy from the melt increases its coercive field relative to slow cooling.
Rapid quenching introduces a higher density of lattice defects.
Rapid quenching introduces increased internal strain.
Lattice defects and internal strain act as pinning sites for magnetic domain walls.
Conventionally slow-cooled magnetic high-entropy alloys have a well-relaxed equilibrium microstructure.
A cooling rate on the order of 10^3 K/s or higher is sufficient to freeze in non-equilibrium defect structures.
The alloy composition and processing atmosphere should be held constant when comparing rapid quenching with slow cooling.
Rapid quenching increases the densities of dislocations and vacancies.
Additional domain-wall pinning centers increase coercivity.
Rapid-quenched samples will exhibit a wider magnetic hysteresis loop corresponding to higher coercivity than matched slow-cooled samples.
Slow cooling produces an equilibrium defect density and lower coercivity than rapid quenching.
Cooling below the necessary rate may fail to retain non-equilibrium defect structures.
Post-quench thermal relaxation may reduce the coercivity enhancement.
Subsequent thermal or magnetic cycling may limit sustained coercivity enhancement.
The magnitude of the coercivity increase depends on alloy composition and quenching parameters.
TEM or X-ray diffraction strain analysis can be used to compare defect-related microstructural changes between quenched and slow-cooled samples.
VSM or SQUID magnetometry can be used to compare coercive fields between quenched and slow-cooled samples.
